title: The Third Letter of John
subtitle: Iōannou Γ, “Third of John”
description: The shortest book in the Bible, a personal note from “the elder” to his dear friend Gaius, and a window into the everyday life of the first churches. Gaius has opened his home to travelling believers who set out for the sake of the Name and take nothing from the pagans; Diotrephes, who loves to be first, has shut his door to them and driven out those who would help. Do not copy what is bad, the elder writes, but what is good; and the rest he will say face to face. In the Open Word Bible, a new translation from the Greek given freely to the public domain, with an introduction to the letter’s shape and meaning and a conclusion on where to read next.

qa.question: What is the Third Letter of John?
qa.answer: The twenty-fifth book of the New Testament and the shortest book in the Bible, a personal letter from “the elder” to a Christian named Gaius. It praises Gaius for welcoming and supporting travelling preachers, rebukes a church leader named Diotrephes who refused to receive them, and commends a man named Demetrius. It is the only book of the New Testament that does not mention Jesus or Christ by name, speaking instead of “the Name” (1:7).

qa.question: Who wrote 3 John, and who were Gaius, Diotrephes and Demetrius?
qa.answer: The writer calls himself “the elder”, as in 2 John, and the two letters are so alike that they are generally agreed to come from the same hand; the church has linked them with John the apostle, though some early Christians thought the elder might be another John. Gaius was a faithful believer, otherwise unknown, who gave hospitality to travelling missionaries. Diotrephes was a leader who “loves to be first” and would not receive them or the elder. Demetrius, well spoken of by everyone, may have carried the letter.

qa.question: What does 3 John teach about hospitality and supporting missionaries?
qa.answer: The travelling believers had set out “for the sake of the Name” and would take nothing from unbelievers, so they relied on the churches for food, lodging and supplies. The elder tells Gaius to send them on “in a manner worthy of God” (1:6) and says that those who take in and support such people “become fellow workers with the truth” (1:8). Those who give share in the work of those who go.

qa.question: Which translation of the Bible is this?
qa.answer: The Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Greek and dedicated to the public domain, printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. The reasoning behind each of its sentences, with the Greek beside it, is published at openwordbible.org. The introduction and conclusion were written for this edition.
